en: *Chaihai Jijie Chao* (Excerpts from the Collected Writings on Measuring the Sea), compiled by Peng Shaosheng, a private disciple of Ji Qing.
This section contains seven poems on the sacred virtues of the successive dynasties, each consisting of several stanzas. Now, one stanza is recorded here: [The Reign of] Shizong.
From the "Chapter on Honoring Sacred Virtue":
"There is brilliance; sagacity constitutes sanctity. His Majesty the Emperor was enlightened in regulating affairs, stern in governing officials, and magnanimous in winning the hearts of the masses.
He revered Heaven and was diligent in governance, never indulging in idle rest. Entrusting matters to the worthy and capable, all affairs were brought to order. His spirit...
His will was clear and pure; thus he was able to intuitively grasp the source of the Way and ascend the path to the realm of the sages (Fifth Chapter).
He did not linger in the fields, nor did he loiter in his chamber; dwelling in profound silence, who could perceive his traces? Thus he roamed the ocean of righteousness.
He has thus penetrated the source of the Dharma, which is vast and boundless; who can truly know how it is so?
"Verses in Commemoration of the Worthy," one hundred and sixty pieces in total; now ten or more are recorded here.
Compiled by Jiao-chao Hu-chen (a native of Jin-tan in Jiang-nan, jinshi of the fourth year of the Shun-zhi era).
Hu Chen was by nature simple and detached. He abstained from meat and blood and delighted in friendships beyond formal circles. While residing in the capital, he attended upon Master Dabo.

One day, while entering court, he heard the sound of the Master chanting the Way and attained a sudden realization. He went to Dabo to present his understanding; after Dabo had examined him repeatedly, he approved.

Subsequently, Hu Chen served as the Superintendent of Education for Shuntian, where his integrity and prudence won the hearts of the scholars. Upon the completion of his term, he submitted his resignation.

He returned home, passed through Baiquan, paid his respects to Sun Zhongyuan, and departed for Mount Lu. He visited Lumen and eventually reached Mount Emei, where he resided at Fuhu Temple. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill;
he wrote a letter to bid farewell to his relatives and friends, sat upright while composing a poem, and passed away.

The following day, a man named Hu encountered him on a mountain peak; he called out "Master Jiang" repeatedly, but there was no response. Upon entering the temple, he learned that [the Master had been taken by] a tiger.
When the minister had already died, [the Emperor] was greatly startled.
Amidst piled-up snow that sealed the dark cliffs and the scattered tracks of tigers and leopards, who could have cast off their official robes and caps to come here and lie upon these flat rocks?

I happened to drink Zhaozhou’s tea; returning, I still carry the sandals from the Onion Range. In the mountain stream, there remains a lingering melody, as the cold, azure waters murmur and cleanse with a clear, tinkling sound.
By the Hanlin Academician Cao Benrong (a native of Huanggang, Hubei, who passed the jinshi examination in the sixth year of the Shunzhi era).
When Benrong was young, he was fond of the writings of Wang Yangming. Upon entering the Hanlin Academy, he was inspired by his tutor, Hu Cihan.

He retired and reflected deeply for one year, after which he attained a sudden and profound realization. He was subsequently appointed as the Superintendent of the Imperial Academy (*Siyè*), where he championed the study of orthodox learning as a model for the six academies.
In the tenth month of winter in the ninth year of the Shunzhi era, he responded to an imperial decree to address matters of state; his memorial was received but not acted upon.

In the fourth month of the twelfth year, the practice of daily lectures (*rìjiǎng*) was instituted, and seven scholars from the Hanlin Academy were appointed as Daily Lecture Officials (*rìjiǎng guān*). Mùxīn was among them. He was later promoted to Left Attendant-in-Ordinary (*zuò shùshì*).
In the ninth month of the fourteenth year of the Zizhi reign, the Imperial Lecture Hall (Jingshan) was first established, and Mu Xin was appointed as a Lecturer at the Jingshan.
He was subsequently promoted to the rank of Attendant Scholar of the National History Academy (Guoshiyuan Shidu Xueshi). Requesting leave to return home due to illness, he passed away in Yangzhou.
As he was about to die, he rose, bathed, and adjusted his robes and cap. Observing that the sun was at its zenith, he sat upright and passed away. (Excerpted)

The enlightened sovereign prizes the encouragement of learning; broad benefit arises from a sincere and open mind. A single word establishes the root of governance; throughout the four seas, the royal wind permeates all.

Pondering deeply on the distant legacy of the sages, he holds others accountable to manifest tranquility and harmony. Beholding the transformation of the world—how swift it is! He sits upright as the sun reaches its zenith.
Geng Jie-shi (natives of Dengfeng, Henan; jinshi degree in the eighth year of the Shunzhi era), Vice Director of the Imperial Library, was a man of pure integrity and upright character.

His conduct was earnest and substantial. During the Shunzhi era, he served as a Court Editor (*jianyue*). He was subsequently appointed as the Surveillance Commissioner for Fujian, where his benevolence and credibility were widely practiced.
In the first year of the Kangxi era, he was transferred to the position of Surveillance Commissioner for Jiangxi and Hedong, and later reassigned to direct jurisdiction under the central government.
Daming Dao served in office for one year, during which he resolved over three hundred cases.
Upon the mourning period for his mother, he went to study under Master Sun of Sumen, where he elucidated the correct learning. He restored the Songyang Academy to cultivate scholars.

In the twenty-fifth year, when Tang Kongbo presided over the Court of Imperial Scholars, [Daming Dao] was summoned to serve as Junior Imperial Scholar, concurrently acting as a tutor to the Crown Prince.
Resented by the authorities, he returned home and continued to preside over the teachings at Songyang.
He never ceased his scholarly pursuits and once wrote a letter to Kong Bo, asserting that the Way is rooted in the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean).
One must not harbor even a trace of cleverness, nor cling to any personal opinions, nor display any flash of brilliance. Kong Bo agreed with these words (excerpted).

Jishi (Zhao Zhifeng) refined his conduct as a Confucian scholar; wherever he went, the sound of his benevolence spread. Returning home, he drank from a single ladle, yet his heart remained detached from the world while cherishing the many heroes of his time.

The spiritual phoenix does not hide itself from the world; its sudden appearance startles the flocks of common birds. Two who shared the same heart have now been separated; in the silence of the empty mountains lies our solemn oath.
During the Shunzhi era, Dou Keming (a native of Henei in Henan, a jinshi degree holder of the ninth year of Shunzhi) served as the Sub-prefect of Fenzhou.
He eradicated the violent and bestowed kindness upon the virtuous; people called him "Dou Buddha."
While traveling through Qinzhou, the Governor of the prefecture, harboring ten ingots of gold, watched him as he slept at night and secretly placed them beneath his bed.

Yún Míng discovered this and summoned the Governor to return the gold. Among the Governor’s subordinates was one whose rank was being promoted; a high official used the subordinate’s private affairs to extort a bribe from him.
Yún Míng maintained that it could not be done. Consequently, the official impeached Yún Míng and dismissed him. On the day he left office, the people of Fén remembered him.

The people were so poor that they vied with one another to offer money and silk, yet he would not accept them. From Fen to Guodi, for several hundred li, those who escorted him held incense and flowers along both sides of the road;
some even shed tears. Upon his return, he built a house to serve his parents until his old age. When Yunming was young, he encountered a group of children playing;
he would often sit alone in a dignified posture, watching them with his hands folded in his sleeves. People gauged his character and potential by this.
The direct path is that which Heaven ordains; its vast emptiness is no cause for my anxiety. I burn incense and bow before the Living Buddha; the precepts stand as dense and lofty as the autumn air.
Parting tears fall upon the long road; a pure breeze leads my carriage home. The crowd of children may try to frighten me in vain; with a single laugh, I am atop the green mountains.

Formerly, during the reign of the Shizu (Emperor Shunzhi), in order to rectify the abuses of the Ming dynasty, he issued an edict reprimanding his ministers for seeking fame and buying favor. *Du-bu Xu Yueshan Zuò (a native of Shanyang, Jiangnan; jinshi degree in the sixth year of the Shunzhi era)*.

[The text continues: "In the past, during the era of the Shizu, in order to remedy the deficiencies of the Ming, an imperial decree was issued holding subordinates accountable for their pursuit of reputation and the purchase of popular favor."

An official statement was ordered to be submitted. The various ministers were immediately struck with trepidation and confessed their crimes. Shan Zhuo, the Censor-in-Chief, submitted a memorial stating:

"The spirit and intellectual acumen of these ministers serve only to preserve their reputation and office. Whenever they receive an imperial decree and must report back, they seek only to avoid trouble.

When one examines their original intentions, it is clear that this is not always the case; rather, their sense of awe and dread has turned into a habit of shirking responsibility. As the myriad affairs of state converge, they rely solely upon—"

"Decisions made in isolation concern the prosperity or decline of governance no small measure. I request that when summoning high and low officials for audience, they be permitted to present their views repeatedly and exhaustively.
Relax prohibitions against those who seek a reputation for virtue to encourage those of mediocre capacity; retain the penalty of banishment for those who commit great wickedness.
It would be a great blessing for the empire. (Excerpt).
The virtue of the dragon benefits the center; below they interact, and the Way prospers. Master Xu utters bitter words, his speech treading upon and eradicating the vulgar and narrow.

The management of rivers follows this same principle: when the lower reaches are blocked, the water overflows to the sides. With great wisdom, he lectures on dredging and clearing; reaching the sea, it attains freedom from harm.
Shangshu Tang Bin, styled Kongbo (a native of Suizyang, Henan; jinshi in the ninth year of the Shunzhi era;

posthumously titled Wenzheng), maintained a dignified countenance while serving at court and remained steadfast in his principles from beginning to end. He was loyal to his sovereign and protective of the people, regarding life and death as matters of consequence for these ends.

During the Shunzhi era, he served as a Hanlin Jianshi and was subsequently appointed as the Military Commissioner (Bingbei Dao) of Tongguan. In the seventeenth year of the Kangxi era, because of his extensive...
Xue Hongru was summoned to serve as a Hanlin Academician. His official career reached the rank of Minister of the Ministry of Rites.

In the ninth month of the twenty-sixth year, he was transferred to the post of Minister of Works. In the tenth month, he passed away due to illness. At the time of his death, he instructed his son, Pu, saying:

"You and your brothers must cultivate the heart that arises upon suddenly seeing a child fall into a well, ensuring it manifests from time to time; when it is fully present and perfectly integrated, one can attain [enlightenment]."

Heavenly Virtue. Had he merely followed and appropriated external forms, he would have ultimately been a "village sage" (xiangyuan) of no benefit. His learning comprehensively integrated the traditions of both Zhu Xi and Lu Xiangshan;
he was a successor to the lineage of Mr. Sun of Suzhou. In the first year of the Qianlong era, he was posthumously granted his current honorary title.
Master Tang was a profound Confucian practitioner; his loyalty and integrity penetrated all things. He felt ashamed that even a single man might suffer from being pushed into a ditch.

This man of Xinye was his peer. How could he remain idle in his vast domain? With such ease, he preserved ultimate auspiciousness. Possessing a heart as steadfast as that in the depths of winter, when the time arrived, he bore its fruit.
Xu Dingsheng (Jiangnan Changzhou native; second-class jinshi graduate in the eleventh year of the Shunzhi era) served as the Magistrate of Yucheng during the Kangxi reign.
Upon first taking office, he inquired after the grievances of the people, treating them with kindness like that of a family member.

In the county, there was a particularly wicked slave who relied on his master’s authority to横行 (act with impunity) throughout the local community. Xu Dingsheng flogged him to death and displayed his corpse [in public].
The people sang of his way, saying: "The Bodhisattva transforms himself into a Vajra; those who offend him are cast aside by the roadside.

He examined the household registers of the district and reduced the number of able-bodied men by more than two thousand to lighten the burden of corvée labor. In his leisure time, he would regularly prepare medicine to give to the sick.

Whenever he attended to official business, those with ailments would gather around his desk to recount their sufferings, and he would invariably provide them with excellent medicine before they departed. After three years, the district was transformed through great order.
The people of Sū were few in number during the reign of King Han-yuan. I have composed this "Ode on the Journey to Yu-cheng" to detail those events.
The Vajra and the Bodhisattva are of one essence and possess no dual minds; the tiger is put to shame by them, while benevolent birds chirp in the spring forest.
He was able to act as medicine for the sick, causing those groaning with pain to find relief. For a thousand autumns he traveled through Yu City; his deeds could be inscribed upon the Yunhe zither.
Shen Jinsi, styled Weishan (a native of Qiantang, Zhejiang; jinshi in the thirty-ninth year of the Kangxi era; posthumous title:

Duankuo), the Left Censor-in-Chief, stated that when Weishan was ten years old and studying under a teacher, he would immediately question what "benevolence" (*ren*) actually was. Upon reaching adulthood, he read the works of Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi.

Serene and composed, he attained realization. With deep faith, he practiced with diligence, his conduct becoming increasingly steadfast day by day. He was promoted to the rank of Left Censor-in-Chief and passed away in office.
Throughout his life, he discussed learning while reciting and following the teachings of Lu Qingxian of Danghu;
his discourse and practical applications were also reminiscent of his. (Excerpt).

My vast ambition seeks the Primordial Beginning; hidden in the deep abyss, my spiritual root flourishes. This spiritual root, firm as frost-battered bone, rises upright to push open the Celestial Gate.

Unveiling my breast, I pour forth far-reaching thoughts; blending the soup, I offer my service to receive Your bright grace. My noble conduct is not yet forgotten; upon the lake, I present these fragrant iris roots.
In the first year of the Qianlong era, Sun Jiagan Xiren (a native of Xing County, Shanxi; jinshi degree in the fifty-second year of the Kangxi era; posthumous title:
Wending), who served as the Minister of the Board of Civil Office, was promoted to Left Censor-in-Chief. He submitted a memorial discussing "Three Habits and One Vice," stating in brief:

"When a sovereign’s ears become habituated to what they hear, they come to prefer flattery and loathe straightforwardness; when their eyes become habituated to what they see, they come to prefer sycophancy..."
Evil lies in being obstinate. When the mind habituates itself to what it considers right, it delights in following that path and hates contrariety.

If the root of self-righteousness is not uprooted, then the mechanism of error will lie dormant in the subtle, and its momentum will become irreversible. Even black and white can change their colors, and east and west can exchange their positions.
I pray that Your Majesty, in every moment and every matter, will constantly maintain a heart that dares not be self-righteous, and... [continue].
King Wen gazed toward the Way yet did not see it; Confucius could only hope for freedom from great transgression—these serve as metaphors. The Sovereign received this with appreciation.

His extraordinary spirit stirred his loyal heart, and he cast aside all clouds to pour forth his sincerity. How excellent is the spirit of the remonstrating minister! Ruler and minister together refined and transformed the world.

One rain fell upon all living beings, and throughout the four seas, people recited the words of Sima [Qian]. The *udumbara* flower does not bloom at ordinary times; gazing back to antiquity, my tears fill my eyes.
Governor-General Yu Chenglong Beiming (a native of Yongning, Shanxi,

posthumously titled Qingdun) served as Governor-General of Jiangnan and Jiangxi during the twentieth year of the Kangxi era. He ate coarse grain mixed with vegetables for his daily meals during a year of famine.
He mixed rice husks with rice to make gruel, which his entire family ate; he served it even to guests who arrived.
He told them, "If you practice this according to the Dharma, you will be able to save some to relieve the hungry. In his later years, there were those who reported him with slanderous rumors.
Bei Ding’s heart was moved. At that time, Xiong Wendu had resigned from the相位 (prime ministership) and was residing in Jiangning.
One day, Bei Ding went to visit him at his residence and sat beneath a wutong tree; they spoke of this matter. Wendu said, "Do you also worry about this?
When a man of great character has thoroughly investigated and seen through it, even life and death cannot alter it—how much less so anything else? Bei Ding replied, "What the Master says is correct."
In the following year, he requested leave to retire, but it was not granted. Upon meeting Wen-duan once more, he appeared sorrowful.
Wen-duan said in a stern voice, "Have you already forgotten our words beneath the wutong tree? Not long after, he passed away while serving in office.
When Lord Gong governed Luocheng, he treated the Yao people as his own children; when he defended Wuhuang, he bound the rebels like tethering swine.

His appointment as a Commander-in-Chief was merely routine, yet the taste of his vegetarian fare was more exquisite than ever. Amidst the wind rustling through the wutong trees, our deliberations were finally met with joy.
Yang Bingjing, Gentleman of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (a native of Fengtian, registered in the Zhenghuang Banner), served as Magistrate of Gu'an during the Kangxi era.
He was subsequently transferred to Wanping. When the Shengzu traveled through the southern part of the capital region, he passed through Gu'an.
The old and the young vied with one another to beg for the post of Governor of Jingshan. The Emperor said, "I shall give you instead a fine official post in Gu'an;
how does that sound? A woman said, "Why not give a fine official post to Wanping instead? The Emperor laughed heartily.
He took this to be the truth. He was granted the stipend of a Prefectural Governor and served as the Magistrate of Gu'an County (excerpt).
A good official is like a pearl; those who obtain it fear they may lose it. Who can bear to treat such a position with mere indifference? One sighs deeply over such a lack of basic provision.
In spring, the elm trees cast low shadows upon the eaves; in autumn, the waters rush through the channels with vigor. From the vast and obscure realm, the heavens and sun have suddenly cleared.

Shen Qiyuan (style name Zida), a Gentleman of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (a native of Taicang, Jiangnan, and a jinshi degree holder of the sixtieth year of the Kangxi era), turned to the study of the *Yi jing* in his later years.

He compiled the *Kongyi Jishuo* (Collected Explanations of the Meaning of Confucius) and, in discussing learning, was proficient in both the Zhu and Lu schools. During his illness, he personally transcribed the *Ming...* [text].
Master Dao’s Recorded Sayings state that he said to his friends: "Throughout my life, my studies have found no point of rest. In recent years, day and night, I have examined my own body and mind;
looking upward, I have no cause for shame, and looking downward, I have no cause for regret. Perhaps I have come close to this. When he passed away, he had no other words.
Beans and grain are but ordinary flavors, yet they serve as a means to sustain life; when famine strikes once more, one extends a hand to revive the weary and infirm.

There is indeed a profound purpose in sincere seeking; the solitary figure beneath the duvet leaves a pure wind to flow on. A single scroll of a book from Luochuan—observing the transformations of the world, there is neither beginning nor end.
The Retired Scholar Sun Qifeng Qitai (a native of Rongcheng, Zhili; a jinshi degree holder during the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty).
During the Tianqi era, Qitai associated with the Donglin Party members and became renowned throughout the world for his integrity and moral resolve.

Later, he increasingly withdrew from public life and concealed himself. His learning followed the school of Wang Yangming, yet he returned to the fundamental principle of "cautiousness in solitude" (*shendu*). He first resided on Mount Wugong. Once...
He crossed the river and stayed at Sūmen. Upon entering our dynasty, he repeatedly declined imperial summons and led his followers in manual cultivation.
He practiced the rites of the Three Dynasties and guided people—whether noble or humble—to do good. Far and near, all were moved by his influence. He passed away at the age of ninety-two.
In surging waves there are no still scales; in fierce winds there are no resting branches. The man of realization sheds himself from the myriad things, coming and going unrestrained.
Guarding the One, he transcends hearing and seeing; his skillful guidance knows no barriers. He silently breathes forth the wind of ritual courtesy, opening this era of Great Peace.
The Retired Scholar Li Yong (Zhongfu), a native of Zhōuwū, Shǎnxī.

The learning of Zhongfu took the realization of innate knowledge (*liangzhi*) as its core principle. He would sit in silent meditation to clarify his mind, reforming his faults and shifting toward goodness as if he were never doing enough.
While traveling in Jiangdong, he lectured on learning for his juniors, often causing them deep and poignant introspection. During the Kangxi era... [text ends]
The officials recommended him to the court, wishing to compel him to take office; however, he firmly declined on the grounds of illness, even going so far as to draw his sword and stab himself.
Thereupon, he took leave of his students and retired to live in a small earthen chamber for the remainder of his life.
The Master closed himself within the chamber of earth; immersed in profound stillness, he distanced himself from worldly fame. The light of Heaven broke forth in the middle of the night;

his innate knowledge shone with brilliant clarity. He fulfilled the duties of a filial son and loyal subject; he was entirely devoid of feelings regarding birth and death. Remaining only the wind of long-nurtured cultivation, he embraced all eminent talents wherever he went.
The Retired Scholar Xie Wenjian, Chunjiu (a native of Nanfeng in Jiangnan; a provincial student during the late Ming dynasty), initially studied Chan Buddhism.
While in quiet meditation, he attained a sudden and clear realization. Subsequently, however, he devoted himself to the teachings of Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi.

He established the Chengshan Academy and, together with his fellow students, urged them toward inner cultivation, taking the single phrase "fearing the mandate of Heaven" as their core method of practice.
At that time, the Nine Sons of Yitang in Ningdu were renowned for their literary talent and statecraft.
However, after Cheng Shan had been lecturing on the learning of the Way for over ten days, all the sons submitted to his wisdom like the autumn waters. (Excerpted)
Accumulated emerald hues lock the perilous cliffs; I open my breast to discuss the ancient *I Ching*. Who is it that excels at washing the mind? A single departure leaves no lingering trace.
Body and name vanish like drifting winds; blowing a whistle, the four walls are empty. Seeking the source, the path does not diverge; I crane my neck as the light of heaven turns white.
The Retired Scholar Wang Fǒng (style name Wèiměi; a jinshi graduate of the Chóngzhèng era of the Ming dynasty from Qiántán, Zhèjiāng) was a man of broad and open character.
He lived in seclusion together with his wife and delighted in traveling to various famous mountains.
He served the monk Sānyí with great reverence, yet he refused to don monastic robes, saying, "I cannot bear to see the Confucian school become empty and devoid of people. When he was nearing death...
He composed a chapter of a five-character poem, ceased writing, and passed away. The poem says: "The Great Transformation knows no resting track;
The paths of the Way have long diverged. Dwelling in this world, I guard my stubborn form; Yet I have not yet fully traversed the road. The Perfected Person fundamentally moves by spiritual power;

It can be realized, but cannot be described. When the ice melts, the water returns to its clarity; When the clouds part, the moon is finally pure. One day, breaking free from the cage, I shall wander at ease."
This is distinct.
Wei Mei is like a wild crane; mountains and rivers offer no fixed dwelling. Looking back upon the space between the pestle and mortar, plum blossoms gleam within my humble hut.
Grasping a mirror to behold my graying hair, I wish to depart yet linger in hesitation. Once the cage is shattered, one is liberated and returns to the Great Void.
The retired scholar Xu Fangzhao (style name Shofa; a native of Changzhou in Jiangnan, who was a *zhusheng* during the Zhengde era of the Ming dynasty) was poor.
Having encountered the turmoil of war and rebellion, he withdrew into the mountains, wearing coarse cloth and straw sandals, never entering a city or town for the rest of his life.

In his later years, Wan Zhi’s commitment to the Way was quite earnest. Once, while visiting Lingyan Mountain to pay respects to Master Tu’eng and inquire about the Buddha-dharma, he found himself destitute and without food.
Master Tu’eng provided him with grain, which he accepted; it was only from Master Tu’eng that he would accept such things.
When Minister Tang Wenzheng arrived there incognito, having screened his carriage and attendants, he was unable to see him and departed with a deep sigh.
A single moon over Lingyan Mountain; autumn frost reflects its solitary purity. The robes of high office dare not gaze upon it; mountain monks share its life. Eating ferns, what cause for resentment?
Plucking chrysanthemums, one finds self-glory. The ocean of learning flows on without ceasing; its vast sentiment endures through all eternity.
The Retired Scholar Zhang Guangwei, alias Cimin (a native of Wuxi, Jiangnan; a provincial graduate during the late Ming dynasty).
Cimin was enrolled as a provincial graduate while still a child. After the fall of the Ming, he wailed before the Confucian Temple and discarded his scholar’s robes.

In his fifties, having lost all his wife and children, he read Buddhist scriptures and practiced the *nienfo* samādhi. Clad in plain cloth and subsisting on simple vegetables, he maintained the precepts.
Regarding the Upāsaka precepts, he was so cautious as to fear harming even a single mosquito or ant.

When he was over seventy years old and about to pass away, he established his final instructions, declaring that he had no worldly concerns or attachments, no anger or afflictions, and that his mind was pure; when the time came, he would simply depart.
His disciples carved his writings into four volumes, titled *Jingtu Shengyan* (Remnants of Words on the Pure Land).

With one great wail, I bid farewell to my scholar’s robes; turning my body, I bow to the Golden Immortal. Who would have known that the ferns of Shouyang Peak had been transformed into lotuses at Donglin?

My flesh and blood lie distant in another world; with incense and flowers, I pass these remaining years. As I depart, there is nothing to grasp—when the moon reaches the center of the sky, it is full.
The Recluse Bi Qi Zilan (a native of Xi County, Jiangnan) had, in his youth, read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and placed his faith in the Great Dharma.
Later, he entered Mashou Mountain, where he met an extraordinary monk who instructed him to seek the ultimate truth.
After five years of arduous investigation, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He then traveled to Wumen and resided there.
Zhiyan dwelt at Dayun Monastery, sitting in meditation all day long. Whenever family members arrived, he would invariably withdraw to avoid them; even when his son died, he did not weep.

He eventually spent the rest of his life in the monastery, composing several scrolls of the *Biézhuàn lù* (Record of Separate Biographies). His wisdom and eloquence were unimpeded, and he was earnestly devoted to helping others.

In a fleeting glance, a speck of dust flies; through causes and conditions, the three realms of existence are conjured like an illusion. Who can suddenly unveil the fundamental light and drain away the wine of ignorance?

The spring breeze carries the fragrance of yellow tubers; the night moon echoes the roar of the Pu-lao bell. With a wave of the hand, I bid farewell to wife and children; in the human world, there is nothing more to pair with me.

The retired scholar Deng Yuanchang (a provincial student from Ganzhou, Jiangxi), whose courtesy name was Mulaan, was twenty-five years old when he obtained the writings of the Five Masters of the Song dynasty.
He then resolved with fervor to pursue learning and subsequently abandoned his studies for the civil service examinations.

In his later years, his realization became even more mature. He once wrote a poem that says: "In every place there is a Peach Blossom Spring, and in every place there is a ferry; one does not know..."
Who is this man from Wuling? From now on, I shall grow weary of asking the fisherman. All day long, I frequently nod off by the window;
my heart is entirely free of stinginess. My conversation harmonizes with children; looking back upon my courtyard, a gentle spring breeze flows of its own accord.
Bowing my head, I reflect upon the long-lost scrolls; I cultivate my practice with a heart stirred by profound sorrow. Peach blossoms fill the mountain stream; who can fathom the source of its path?
In the *Preface to the Compendium for Measuring the Sea*, Confucius said: "How great was Yao as a ruler! How majestic! Only Heaven is great; only Yao emulated it."
Thus it is. Yet those of antiquity who praised Yao said, "He neither knows nor understands," and "What power does the Emperor have?
Master Zeng (Dongguo) said, "All day long I wear the sky upon my head, yet I do not know its height. Is this not indeed so? Is this not indeed so?
I have the good fortune to have been born and raised in an age of governance, inheriting the legacy of my ancestors and basking in their benevolent grace.
Singing the praises of this era of Great Peace, I have privately composed seven poems on the Sagely Virtue of Our Dynasty, supplemented by one hundred and sixty "Eulogies for the Worthy.
I have titled this collection *Cheshai Ji* (Measuring the Sea). Now, the sea cannot be measured, just as heaven cannot be fully known. To attempt to measure it— [The text ends here.]
"What can be done? It is simply a matter of not-knowing and not-understanding," it is said. "It is simply a matter of asking what power the Sovereign possesses," it is also said.
The singing of Yao today is just like the singing of Yao in antiquity. Written on the first day of the fourth month of summer in the forty-fourth year of the Qianlong era by Peng Shaosheng.
